tagline.text: The tuna capital's first-week-of-September festival of floats and street grills

location.label: Location
location.text: Pioneer Avenue, Oval Plaza and the Fish Port area, General Santos City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱8,000–20,000 (including flights from Manila, 2 nights and 3 days, per person, estimated)

children.text: The Tuna Festival is a roughly week-long celebration that General Santos, the center of the Philippine tuna industry, holds in the first week of September every year. In one city you can see tuna-themed float parades, tuna grilled right in the street, events at the fish port, and a closing on the city's charter anniversary.

The Tuna Festival is a city festival held every year in the first week of September in General Santos (locally called GenSan), in South Cotabato in southern Mindanao. Wikipedia describes it as a week-long festival that combines a float parade decorated with tuna themes, street dancing and food events, and says it has run since 1998. Some event guides give the first festival as September 5, 1999, so sources differ by about a year on the start. Either way, it has been the city's signature event for more than 20 years.

The festival falls in early September because the city's charter anniversary is September 5. General Santos became a city under Republic Act No. 5412 in 1968, and its first anniversary celebration is said to have been held on September 5 of that year. That is why the last day of the Tuna Festival is usually the charter anniversary closing, and the day is often declared a special non-working holiday. One account says the anniversary and the festival dates were run separately around 2017, so details can change from year to year. The safest way to confirm the exact dates is the schedule the city government usually publishes in mid-August.

The reason this city holds a tuna festival is its industry. The General Santos Fish Port Complex is one of the country's leading fishing ports, and tuna canneries and processors are clustered around the city. One travel guide says the city handles about 90 percent of the Philippines' tuna volume, but it gives no source, so treat that as the pride the city claims rather than a verified figure. The Wikipedia article also mentions a record tuna catch of 33.6 tonnes. The festival began as a way to thank the tuna industry, its fishermen and its processing workers.

For visitors the festival has two main draws. One is the parades and music events centered on Pioneer Avenue by day and night. The other is that you can eat as much tuna as you like. From tuna collar and belly grilled in the street to sashimi at the fish port and tuna pastil from roadside stalls, the whole city becomes a tuna food fair. The program is concentrated in a few spots downtown, so with a little preparation for traffic closures and hotel bookings you can comfortably do it as a 2-night, 3-day trip from Manila.

Floats topped with giant tuna and other sea creatures roll through downtown and are the face of the festival. Wikipedia describes it as a colorful parade showing marine life. One event guide says that on the opening day,
September 1
, it takes place in the evening around Oval Plaza and Pioneer Avenue, so check the exact time each year.

A long line of grills fills Pioneer Avenue in this street-grilling event. Wikipedia describes it as a display of grilled tuna panga (collar), prawns and other seafood, and one guide calls it an open-air grill stretching about
1 km
. According to the same guide, free tastings sponsored by local fishing companies follow.

blocks.title: Fish port party and Linis Tuna

children.text: At the fish port, the Grand Fish Fest sa Fishport takes place, along with the Linis Tuna contest for the fastest tuna cleaner and the Buhat Tuna contest to find the mightiest fisherman. They turn fishermen's everyday skills into sport, which makes them fun to watch.

According to one event guide, on the third day of the festival an outrigger boat race called Bankarera is held at sea. The roads to the coast can get congested from late morning, so it is best to head out early.

Lawi-Lawi sa GenSan is a street parade in which local schools and groups perform in colorful costumes and compete in dance. It is the biggest spectacle and it costs nothing to watch, so people start claiming spots on the Pioneer Avenue sidewalk early.

According to Wikipedia, a Tuna Culinary and Skills Olympics is also held. It is a contest of tuna cutting and cooking skills, and food bazaars on Roxas East and Pendatun Avenues let you taste tuna dishes cheaply.

An opening concert and fireworks on the opening day, then a cultural show and fireworks for the charter anniversary on the last day, follow one another at Oval Plaza. Wikipedia reports that in 2024, for the 56th anniversary of cityhood, there were fireworks and a performance by well-known entertainers.

children.text: Fly from Manila to General Santos in about
2 hours
and drop your bags at the hotel. Rooms fill up early in festival week, so it is easiest to stay near Pioneer Avenue and keep the afternoon close to it.
Head to Oval Plaza and Pioneer Avenue for the opening ceremony and the float parade. The sidewalk fills up around
for the evening parade, so claim a spot 1–2 hours early.
If you can, go to the fish port in the Tambler district around
. You need to arrive early to see the unloading and grading. Shorts and sandals may be refused entry, so wear long pants and closed shoes.

Watch the fish port events and contests such as Linis Tuna and Buhat Tuna, and try tuna sashimi or kinilaw at the stalls. On days when the Bankarera race is held, the coastal road is congested, so allow extra time.
Walk Pioneer Avenue on the evening of Sugbahan sa Dalan. Taste grilled tuna panga and prawns, and end the day with a music show.
If it is the day of the charter anniversary closing, watch the cultural show and fireworks at Oval Plaza. If you book a late-afternoon flight home, you can fit in one more daytime event.
The program changes from year to year. Adjust the order above according to the official schedule published by the city government.

Pioneer Avenue is often closed to vehicles on the opening day and on the street-grill day. Leave your car at the hotel and go on foot.

The Tuna Festival is held in the first week of September every year, and that is the only time to see it. It closes on September 5, the city's charter anniversary. Check the schedule the city government usually publishes in mid-August for exact dates and the program.

September is the middle of the rainy season in the Philippines, but southern Mindanao, where General Santos lies, is usually away from typhoon tracks. Even so, afternoon showers are frequent, so bring an umbrella and a light rain jacket. Outdoor parades may be reordered if it rains.

Staying within about 15 minutes by tricycle of Pioneer Avenue and Oval Plaza is convenient. One festival guide says cheap rooms are gone by around July in festival week and mid-range rooms rise above ₱3,000. Even if the exact numbers are hard to verify, the point that you should book at least two to three months ahead holds. Hotels mentioned downtown include Greenleaf Hotel, Grand Summit Hotel and Microtel, and budget rooms in the RedDoorz chain are quoted at around ₱1,000–2,000.

Food is half of this festival. Tuna pastil at about ₱10 from roadside stalls, tuna kinilaw at the food bazaars, and grilled tuna belly and roe dishes at seafood restaurants are all worth trying. One guide recommends Nikolai Seafood House for tuna belly and roe, and Tiongson Arcade as a night-market eatery where you pick fish from the ice and have it grilled. When you eat seafood, check the freshness with your own eyes and ask the price first.
Check the official schedule the city government publishes in mid-August, then book flights and a hotel to match the dates.
Arrive 1–2 hours early for the evening parade to get a good spot on the Pioneer Avenue sidewalk.
Visit the fish port in the early morning. Shorts, sandals and sleeveless tops may be refused entry, so wear long pants and closed shoes and bring ID.
Boots can reportedly be rented near the fish port entrance, so check the price on the spot.
Bring plenty of cash. Roadside stalls, tricycles and jeepneys mostly take cash only.
September brings frequent showers, so a compact umbrella and a light rain jacket are useful.
Agree on the fare before boarding a tricycle. Downtown has many closed sections during events, so walking is often faster.
Festival schedules and traffic closures change every year, so check the General Santos city government's notices again just before you leave.
The schedule, traffic closures and ticket prices change every year, so be sure to check the city government's latest notices before you go.
Hotels and flights sell out early in festival week. Last-minute bookings are expensive or simply unavailable.
Venues get crowded. Keep your phone and wallet in a front pocket and do not hold them in your hand for long.
The fish port is a place of work. Follow the dress rules and photography guidance, and do not get in the way of workers.
Travel safety information for Mindanao can change. Before you leave, check your government's travel advisory and local news.
Check the hygiene of street seafood with your own eyes before eating, and choose cooked food if you have a sensitive stomach.
You can find an introduction to the host city itself and how to get around in its own entry. From downtown, take a tricycle to the fish port.
A beach along the Sarangani coast running south from General Santos, a good place to rest for a day after the festival.
A lake in the mountains of South Cotabato, a candidate if you want to add a nature outing to the festival. The travel time is long, so plan it as a separate trip.
A highland lake and T'boli cultural area in the west of South Cotabato, which you visit from General Santos with at least a full day.
